title: Soil exploration, earth pressure and retaining structures
summary: Two topics share this subchapter. Soil exploration is largely factual — the SPT procedure and its corrections, sampler quality, depth of exploration — and rewards exact recall of numbers. Earth pressure rests on three coefficients whose order (K_a < K_0 < K_p) should be as automatic as knowing which way water flows; get that ordering and the direction of wall movement right, and most questions answer themselves. For retaining walls, the four stability checks and the central role of drainage are the reliable marks.

sections.heading: Soil exploration — purpose, extent and methods
sections.body:
**Purpose:** to determine the **stratification**, the **engineering properties** of each stratum, the **groundwater** conditions, and the presence of any **problem soil** (expansive, collapsible, organic, liquefiable, contaminated).

**Depth of exploration** should be at least **1.5 to 2 times the width** of the loaded area — because the significant stress increase, the **20% isobar**, extends to about that depth. Below it the added stress is too small to cause appreciable settlement.

Specific rules:

| Situation | Depth |
|---|---|
| **Isolated footing** | 1.5 – 2 × width B |
| **Raft** | 1.5 – 2 × the **shorter** dimension |
| **Pile group** | 1.5 × the width **below the pile tips** |
| Adjacent footings whose pressure bulbs overlap | Treat as a single larger loaded area |
| Rock encountered | 3 m into sound rock, to confirm it is not a boulder |

The last is worth stating: a **boulder can be mistaken for bedrock**, with expensive consequences, so penetration must confirm continuity.

**Number and spacing** of boreholes: typically **10–30 m** for a building, closer where conditions are erratic. The governing principle is that boreholes must be enough to **interpolate confidently between them** — which depends on the variability found, not on a fixed rule.

**Methods of exploration:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Trial pit / trench** | Direct visual inspection; **shallow only** (up to ~3 m) but the most informative per rupee |
| **Auger boring** | Hand or power; above the water table in cohesive soil |
| **Wash boring** | Fast, cheap; **cuttings are washed up so stratification is poorly identified** |
| **Percussion boring** | Boulders and hard strata; disturbs the soil considerably |
| **Rotary drilling** | Rock coring; gives an **undisturbed rock core** and the **RQD** |
| **Geophysical** — seismic refraction, electrical resistivity | **Rapid, non-intrusive, covers large areas**; indirect, so it needs calibration against boreholes |

**Geophysical methods** are complementary rather than alternative: they interpolate cheaply between boreholes over a large site, but cannot replace a sample.

**Sampling quality.** The measure is the **area ratio**:

> **A_r = (D_o² − D_i²)/D_i² × 100%**

| Sampler | Area ratio | Sample |
|---|---|---|
| **Thin-walled (Shelby) tube** | **< 10%** | **Undisturbed** |
| Piston / stationary piston sampler | < 10% | Undisturbed, soft clay |
| **Split-spoon (SPT)** | **> 100%** | **Disturbed** only |
| Denison, Pitcher | Moderate | Undisturbed in stiff soil |

Also specified: **inside clearance 0.5–3%** (so the sample does not bind in the tube) and **outside clearance 0–2%** (to reduce driving friction).

**Why it matters:** index tests (water content, limits, grading) can be run on **disturbed** material, but **strength and consolidation tests cannot** — they need the soil's in-situ structure. Requesting a triaxial test on a split-spoon sample is a category error.

sections.heading: The Standard Penetration Test
sections.body:
The most widely used field test, because it is quick, cheap and correlates with a great many properties.

**Procedure:** a **split-spoon sampler** is driven by a **63.5 kg hammer falling 750 mm**, through **450 mm** in three 150 mm increments.

> **N = the number of blows for the LAST 300 mm** (the second and third increments)

The **first 150 mm is the seating drive and is discarded**, because the base of the borehole is disturbed by the drilling. Missing that is the single commonest error about the test.

The test is stopped at **50 blows** for any increment — recorded as refusal.

**Corrections**, applied in this order:

| Correction | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Overburden pressure** | The same sand gives a higher N at depth simply because it is more confined |
| **Dilatancy** (fine sand or silt below water) | Negative pore pressure during driving inflates N |
| Energy, rod length, borehole diameter, sampler type | Equipment differences |

**Dilatancy correction (IS 2131)**, for fine sand and silt below the water table:

> **N_c = 15 + ½(N − 15)** when N > 15;  no correction when N ≤ 15

**Interpretation:**

| N | Sand | N | Clay (consistency) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 – 4 | Very loose | < 2 | Very soft |
| 4 – 10 | Loose | 2 – 4 | Soft |
| 10 – 30 | Medium | 4 – 8 | Medium |
| 30 – 50 | Dense | 8 – 15 | Stiff |
| > 50 | Very dense | 15 – 30 | Very stiff |
| | | > 30 | Hard |

**Correlations** drawn from N: relative density, **φ**, allowable bearing pressure, settlement, and **liquefaction susceptibility** — the last being why the test is mandatory for Kathmandu Valley sites under NBC 105.

**Its limitations are real and worth knowing**, because questions ask when *not* to rely on it. N is **highly operator- and equipment-dependent**; it is **unreliable in gravel** (a single stone jams the sampler and gives a spuriously high N) and **in soft clay** (where the blow count is too small to resolve). For clays the **vane shear** or a laboratory triaxial test is far better; for gravels a **plate load test** or geophysical method.

**Other field tests:**

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Static cone penetration (CPT)** | Continuous **cone resistance and sleeve friction** — a continuous profile, no borehole needed |
| **Dynamic cone penetration** | Rapid profiling, correlated with N |
| **Plate load test** | **Bearing capacity and settlement** directly, but only to a shallow depth |
| **Vane shear** | Undrained strength of soft clay |
| **Pressuremeter** | In-situ stress–strain and modulus |

The **CPT's advantage** is that it gives a **continuous** record, so a thin weak layer that a borehole at 1.5 m intervals would miss entirely is detected. Its limitation is that it recovers **no sample**.

**Plate load test caution:** the plate is small (300–750 mm), so its pressure bulb is shallow. It therefore gives a good indication for **sand** (where settlement is immediate and shallow) but is **misleading for clay**, because it cannot detect a compressible layer below its own influence zone. Settlement must be scaled: **S_footing/S_plate = B_footing/B_plate** for sand, and equal for clay.

sections.heading: Earth pressure theory
sections.body:
**Three states**, and their ordering must be automatic:

| State | Coefficient | Wall movement | Magnitude |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Active** | **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)** | Wall moves **AWAY** from the backfill | **Smallest** |
| **At rest** | **K_0 = 1 − sin φ** (Jaky) | **No** movement | Intermediate |
| **Passive** | **K_p = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = 1/K_a** | Wall moves **INTO** the backfill | **Largest** |

> **K_a < K_0 < K_p** always

For **φ = 30°**: K_a = **1/3**, K_0 = **0.5**, K_p = **3**. Those three numbers are worth memorising as a check on any computed value.

Equivalently, **K_a = tan²(45° − φ/2)** and **K_p = tan²(45° + φ/2)**.

**Why the direction of movement decides which applies.** **Active** pressure is the soil *pushing* the wall — the soil is the actor, and it mobilises its own strength to resist collapse, so the pressure is reduced below at-rest. **Passive** pressure is the wall *pushing* the soil — the soil resists, and its full strength is mobilised against the wall, so the pressure is greatly increased.

**The movement required is very different**, and this has a practical consequence:

| State | Movement to mobilise |
|---|---|
| **Active** | Small — about **0.001 to 0.005 H** |
| **Passive** | Large — about **0.01 to 0.05 H**, roughly **ten times** more |

Because passive resistance needs so much movement, the passive resistance of soil in front of a wall is often **discounted or heavily factored** in design: by the time it is fully mobilised the structure has moved unacceptably.

**Pressure distribution and resultant** for a dry cohesionless backfill of height H:

> **p_a = K_a γ z**  (triangular)
> **P_a = ½ K_a γ H²**,  acting at **H/3 above the base**

The resultant sits at the centroid of the triangle. A **uniform surcharge q** adds a **rectangular** block **K_a q** acting at **H/2**. A **submerged** backfill contributes **K_a γ′ H** from the soil **plus the full hydrostatic γ_w H** — and the water pressure is **not** reduced by K_a, which is a frequent and dangerous error.

**Cohesive backfill:**

> **p_a = K_a γ z − 2c√K_a**

The cohesion term is **negative**, so the pressure is **negative (tensile) near the top** down to a depth

> **z_0 = 2c/(γ√K_a)**

Soil cannot sustain tension against the wall, so a **tension crack** forms to that depth. If the crack fills with water the wall receives full hydrostatic pressure over it — which is exactly why **clay backfill is a poor choice** and why drainage matters so much.

**Rankine versus Coulomb:**

| | **Rankine** | **Coulomb** |
|---|---|---|
| Wall friction | **Ignored** (smooth wall) | **Included** (δ) |
| Wall back | Vertical | May be **inclined** |
| Backfill surface | Level or uniformly sloping | Any |
| Failure surface | Planar | Planar |
| Character | Simpler; **conservative for active** | More general |

**Coulomb's passive value is unsafe** for large wall friction, because the real failure surface is **curved**, not planar — so the planar assumption overestimates the resistance. Rankine's active value is safe to use because ignoring wall friction overestimates the thrust slightly.

sections.heading: Retaining structures
sections.body:
**Types**, in order of increasing height and sophistication:

| Type | Resists by | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravity wall** (masonry, mass concrete) | Its **own weight** | Low walls, up to ~3 m |
| **Cantilever wall** (RCC, L or T stem) | Weight plus the **weight of soil on the base slab** | 3 – 8 m |
| **Counterfort wall** | As cantilever, with counterforts on the **earth** side | Over 8 m |
| **Buttress wall** | Counterforts on the **exposed** side | Over 8 m (buttresses are in compression) |
| **Crib / gabion** | Weight, but **flexible and permeable** | Hill roads, river banks |
| **Sheet pile** | Embedment, and anchors or struts | Excavations, waterfronts |
| **Reinforced soil / MSE** | **Tensile reinforcement** within the fill | Tall walls, bridge approaches |
| **Soil nailing, anchors** | Tension into the retained mass | Cuttings, existing slopes |

The **counterfort/buttress** distinction is examined: counterforts are on the **earth** side and act in **tension**; buttresses are on the **exposed** side and act in **compression**, which is structurally better but looks worse and takes usable space.

**The four stability checks**, with minimum factors of safety:

| Check | Minimum F | Governed by |
|---|---|---|
| **Overturning** about the toe | **2.0** | Σ stabilising moments ÷ Σ overturning moments |
| **Sliding** along the base | **1.5** | (ΣV · μ + adhesion) ÷ ΣH |
| **Bearing pressure** at the base | **3.0** on ultimate | p = ΣV/B ± 6ΣV·e/B² |
| **Overall (deep-seated) slope failure** | **1.5** | A slip circle through the wall and foundation |

The **fourth check is the one most often omitted** — a wall can be perfectly stable in itself yet ride down on a slip surface passing beneath it, which is precisely what happens on a hill road built on a marginally stable slope.

For the bearing check, **no tension** should develop at the heel, which requires the resultant to fall within the **middle third** of the base:

> **e ≤ B/6**

the same middle-third rule that governs masonry dams and chimneys.

**Drainage is the single most important detail, and the most neglected.** A wall designed for earth pressure alone and then allowed to accumulate water behind it can receive **two to three times** the design thrust, because hydrostatic pressure is not reduced by K_a. Most retaining wall failures are drainage failures.

The measures:

| Measure | Function |
|---|---|
| **Weep holes** (75–100 mm, at 1–1.5 m centres) | Let water out through the wall |
| **Granular filter / drainage blanket** behind the wall | Conducts water down to the weep holes without clogging |
| **Longitudinal perforated drain** at the base | Collects and carries water away |
| **Geotextile filter** | Prevents fines migrating into the granular layer |
| **Surface sealing** at the crest | Stops infiltration in the first place |

**Backfill choice** follows the same logic: **free-draining granular material is best**. Clay is poor because it holds water, swells, and develops the tension crack described above; and it should never be placed directly behind a wall designed for granular fill.

**Compaction of the backfill** needs care in both directions: too little and the wall settles and the fill subsides; too much and **compaction-induced lateral pressure** can exceed the at-rest value, since heavy rollers working close to the wall push it forward. Light plant is used within about 1 m of the wall.

**Sheet pile walls** are analysed differently, since they rely on **embedment** rather than weight: a **cantilever** sheet pile is suitable to about 5 m, an **anchored** or **strutted** one beyond that. The design finds the depth of embedment giving moment equilibrium about the anchor, with **passive resistance in front** balanced against **active pressure behind** — and the passive value is factored, for the mobilisation reason given above.

formulas.label: Earth pressure coefficients
formulas.expression: K_a = (1−sin φ)/(1+sin φ) = tan²(45−φ/2);  K_0 = 1 − sin φ;  K_p = 1/K_a
formulas.note: K_a < K_0 < K_p always. For φ = 30°: 1/3, 0.5, 3.

formulas.label: Active thrust on a wall
formulas.expression: P_a = ½ K_a γ H², acting at H/3 above the base
formulas.note: A surcharge q adds K_a q acting at H/2. Water adds the FULL γ_w H, not reduced by K_a.

formulas.label: Cohesive backfill and tension crack
formulas.expression: p_a = K_a γ z − 2c√K_a ;   crack depth z_0 = 2c/(γ√K_a)
formulas.note: Soil cannot take tension, so a crack forms. If it fills with water the wall gets full hydrostatic pressure.

formulas.label: SPT and its dilatancy correction
formulas.expression: N = blows for the LAST 300 mm of a 450 mm drive;  N_c = 15 + ½(N − 15) for N > 15
formulas.note: 63.5 kg hammer, 750 mm drop. The first 150 mm seating drive is discarded.

formulas.label: Area ratio of a sampler
formulas.note: Split-spoon exceeds 100%, so it gives a disturbed sample: no strength or consolidation testing.

formulas.label: Retaining wall stability
formulas.note: The overall slope check is the one most often omitted — a stable wall can ride down on a deeper slip surface.

formulas.label: No-tension (middle third) rule
formulas.expression: e ≤ B/6 for a rectangular base;  p = ΣV/B ± 6ΣV·e/B²
formulas.note: The resultant must fall within the middle third so no tension develops at the heel.

formulas.label: Plate load test scaling
formulas.expression: Sand: S_footing/S_plate = B_footing/B_plate.   Clay: settlement independent of width.
formulas.note: The plate's shallow pressure bulb cannot detect a compressible layer deeper down — misleading for clay.
